title: Harbrook Bank: the fraud screening decision
prompt: Card fraud screening works in three steps. Every card transaction is scored as it happens; transactions the model finds suspicious raise an alert; and an alert is only acted on once a human analyst in the fraud operations team reviews it and decides whether to block the transaction and call the cardholder. An alert nobody reviews is released — the transaction goes through, and if it was fraudulent the bank carries the loss. Our client is Harbrook Bank, a large retail bank whose card fraud losses have been climbing for three years, with the regulator watching. Harbrook's fraud operations team can review 500,000 alerts a year, and today's rules-based screening uses 300,000 of them. A vendor has offered Harbrook a machine-learning screening system that is genuinely better at spotting fraud, and the Chief Risk Officer wants to know whether it is worth buying. Two terms will matter today: an alert is only worth raising if someone reviews it, and the number we care about is the incremental benefit — what the new system adds over the rules Harbrook already runs, not what it achieves in total.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — How a fraud alert turns into a prevented loss
exhibits.text: Transaction scored → alert raised → analyst reviews the alert → transaction blocked and cardholder called. The chain only prevents a loss if all four steps happen. Alerts raised beyond what the review team can handle are released unreviewed, and prevent nothing.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — Harbrook's card fraud screening: today's rules and the vendor's system (Scenario 1)

rows: Average value of a fraudulent transaction (USD)
Share of fraud value prevented, if every alert raised is reviewed
Alerts the fraud operations team can review per year

exhibits.unitsNote: The extra alerts the proposed system raises are of uniform quality: reviewing a given share of them prevents that share of the extra fraud value. Alerts that cannot be reviewed are released.
exhibits.source: Fraud operations MI and the vendor's proposal

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — Scenario 2: an offshore partner reviews the overflow

rows: Average value of a fraudulent transaction (USD)
Share of fraud value prevented, if every alert raised is reviewed
Alerts the fraud operations team can review per year

exhibits.unitsNote: Changed from Scenario 1: review capacity is 1,100,000 alerts a year, not 500,000 — an offshore partner would take the overflow at the same $1.50 an alert. Every other figure is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Let's start with the right structure. What are the three key questions you would need to answer in order to tell Harbrook whether to buy the new screening system? Please summarise them in 3 lines maximum.

keyPoints: How much extra fraud would the new system actually prevent, over and above the rules Harbrook already runs?
What does it cost to get that benefit — the licence, and the analyst time needed to review the alerts it raises?
Can the bank deliver it operationally: can the review team handle the alert volume, and what does the regulator require either way?
commonMistakes: Answering with a generic build-versus-buy or cost-benefit framework rather than the three questions this decision turns on.
Framing it as the total fraud the system catches rather than the incremental catch over today's rules.
Ignoring the operational constraint entirely — the alert review capacity is the binding one here.
Naming six things when the interviewer asked for three.

questions.followUp: Good. The vendor has given us its numbers and the fraud operations team has given us theirs. Note that the review team's capacity is shared: alerts from today's rules and alerts from the new system compete for the same analysts.

questions.prompt: Scenario 1: given the data in the exhibit, what is the annual net benefit to Harbrook of switching to the proposed system? Please give your answer rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in USD per year, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working. If the net benefit is negative, enter it with a minus sign, for example -250000.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Fraud exposure: 40,000 attempts × $300 = $12.0M a year.
Today's rules raise 300,000 alerts, all of which fit inside the 500,000 the team can review, and prevent 50% of the fraud value = $6.0M.
The proposed system would prevent 75% = $9.0M, but only if all 900,000 of its alerts were reviewed. The team can review 500,000, of which 300,000 are already spoken for, so only 200,000 of the 600,000 extra alerts get looked at — one third.
Incremental fraud prevented = ($9.0M − $6.0M) × 1/3 = $1.0M.
Incremental review cost = 200,000 × $1.50 = $0.3M.
Licence = $1.5M.
Net benefit = $1.0M − $0.3M − $1.5M = −$800,000 a year. On these figures the system destroys value: the bank would be paying for detection it has no capacity to act on.
keyPoints: The benefit is incremental: what the new system prevents over and above today's $6.0M, not the whole $9.0M.
Detection that is never reviewed prevents nothing, so the benefit is capped by spare review capacity, not by the model's accuracy.
Only the extra alerts carry extra review cost; the first 300,000 are being reviewed already.
commonMistakes: Valuing the benefit at the full $9.0M the system detects and answering $7.2M, forgetting the bank already prevents $6.0M.
Assuming all 900,000 alerts get reviewed and answering $600,000 — that is Scenario 2's answer, not this one.
Charging the review cost on all 500,000 reviewed alerts rather than on the 200,000 incremental ones.
Leaving the licence out of an 'annual net benefit'.

questions.prompt: Please explain briefly the reasoning behind your answer to the previous question, in 3 lines maximum.

keyPoints: Compare the proposed system with today's rules, not with doing nothing: only the extra fraud prevented counts as benefit.
The extra detection has to pass through the review team, and there is only enough spare capacity for one third of the extra alerts, so only one third of the extra benefit is real.
Against that, the incremental review cost and the licence fee, which is paid in full whether or not the alerts get reviewed.
The result is negative, which is the point: the constraint is operational capacity, not model quality.
commonMistakes: Describing the arithmetic without naming the capacity constraint that drives it.
Talking about the model's accuracy as if accuracy alone were the benefit.
Not saying explicitly that the answer is negative and what that implies.

questions.followUp: Understood. For completeness, the vendor's licence is a flat annual fee — it does not vary with alert volumes, and it is payable from day one.

questions.prompt: I'd like to check a couple of the parameters behind that. In Scenario 1, how much additional fraud value would the proposed system actually prevent in a year? Please give your answer rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in USD per year, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Fraud exposure = 40,000 × $300 = $12.0M.
The system would lift prevention from 50% to 75%, worth $3.0M a year if every alert were reviewed.
Extra alerts = 900,000 − 300,000 = 600,000. Spare review capacity = 500,000 − 300,000 = 200,000, so one third of the extra alerts are reviewed.
$3.0M × 1/3 = $1,000,000.
keyPoints: The 25-point improvement is worth $3.0M gross, but only the reviewed share of it lands.
Spare capacity, not total capacity, is what the extra alerts can use.
commonMistakes: Answering $3,000,000 and ignoring the review constraint.
Using 500,000 / 900,000 as the reviewed share, which double-counts the alerts today's rules already consume.
Answering $9,000,000, the total prevented rather than the additional.

questions.followUp: Thanks. The fraud operations director confirms the team is at full utilisation today: there is no slack beyond the 500,000 figure in the exhibit, and no budget approved for more analysts.

questions.prompt: And what is the additional alert review cost the bank would incur in a year under Scenario 1? Please give your answer rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in USD per year, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Only the incremental alerts that actually get reviewed cost anything extra: 200,000 of them.
200,000 × $1.50 = $300,000 a year.
The 300,000 alerts today's rules raise are already being reviewed and already cost $450,000; that cost does not change.
keyPoints: Incremental cost against incremental benefit: the existing review load is unaffected by the decision.
Alerts the team never reviews cost nothing — and prevent nothing.
commonMistakes: Charging all 900,000 alerts at $1.50 and answering $1,350,000.
Charging the full 500,000 reviewed alerts and answering $750,000.
Adding the licence fee into the review cost.

questions.followUp: That is the picture at today's capacity. Before we conclude, the Chief Risk Officer wants to know how robust the number is — several things are still moving.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements, if true, would change the annual net benefit you calculated? Select all that apply.
options: The vendor would drop the flat licence and charge $2.00 for every alert of its system that Harbrook reviews
Fraud attempts are expected to run 20% higher next year, with no change in alert volumes
A competitor bank has just deployed the same vendor's system
The $1.50 per alert is entirely the salary of review analysts whose headcount is fixed for the next two years
The proposed system raises 900,000 alerts a year against today's 300,000

optionRationale: Changes it. The $1.5M licence is replaced by 200,000 reviewed alerts × $2.00 = $400,000, so the net benefit moves from −$800,000 to +$300,000 — and the decision flips. Pricing that scales with what the bank can actually use is worth more to Harbrook than the model is.

Changes it. Exposure rises to $14.4M, so the reviewed third of the 25-point improvement is worth $1.2M rather than $1.0M and the net benefit improves to −$600,000. Still negative: growing fraud does not fix a capacity constraint.
Does not change it. What a competitor buys says nothing about Harbrook's own incremental benefit or its review capacity. It is a reason to ask questions, not a term in this calculation.

Changes it. If the analysts are paid whether or not these alerts exist, the $300,000 is not an incremental cost of the decision at all, and the net benefit improves to −$500,000. Committed cost is not incremental cost.
Does not change it. That is the exhibit restated; both figures are already inside the number you gave.
keyPoints: Test each statement by asking which term of your own calculation it touches.
Committed costs drop out of an incremental calculation; a charge that scales with usage does not.
A bigger problem does not raise the value of a solution the bank cannot operate.
commonMistakes: Picking the competitor's deployment because it feels strategically relevant.
Rejecting the fixed-headcount statement as an accounting detail; it changes what counts as incremental.
Assuming higher fraud must make the system worth buying, without re-running the capped benefit.

questions.followUp: Helpful. One development since we last spoke: procurement has found an offshore partner that would review the overflow alerts at the same $1.50 each, lifting reviewable volume to 1,100,000 a year. Nothing else about the proposal changes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is likely to be true for Scenario 2 compared with Scenario 1? Use the data below for your revised calculation. The change is described under the exhibit.
options: The switch is worth making in Scenario 2, having not been worth making in Scenario 1
The switch remains not worth making, though by a smaller margin
The net benefit is unchanged, because the system's detection rate has not changed
There is not enough information to decide

optionRationale: Correct. With 1,100,000 alerts reviewable, all 600,000 extra alerts get looked at, so the full $3.0M of extra prevention lands. Review cost rises to 600,000 × $1.50 = $0.9M, the licence is still $1.5M, and the net benefit is +$600,000 a year. The model did not improve — the bank's ability to act on it did.
Wrong, and it is the answer you get if you keep the one-third cap from Scenario 1 without re-reading the capacity row.
Wrong. The detection rate is indeed unchanged; that is exactly why this is worth noticing. What changed is how much of that detection reaches a human, which is where the value was being lost.
Wrong. Capacity, alert volumes, prevention rates, review cost and licence are all given. This option deserves real consideration in a case where something is genuinely missing; here nothing is.
keyPoints: −$800,000 becomes +$600,000: a $1.4M swing with no change to the technology.
The binding constraint was review capacity, so relieving it is where the value came from.
$0.9M of review cost buys $3.0M of prevention — the overflow alerts are worth reviewing on their own merits.
commonMistakes: Re-running the whole calculation from scratch and losing the incremental framing.
Assuming more capacity must mean more cost without checking what that cost buys.
Choosing 'not enough information' because the offshore arrangement feels underspecified.

questions.prompt: Please explain in 2 to 3 lines the reasoning behind your answer to the previous question — and say what that implies about where Harbrook's real problem lies.

keyPoints: The system's detection is identical in both scenarios; what changes is how much of it a human ever acts on.
With the overflow reviewed, the full incremental prevention lands and the extra review cost is small against it, so the switch pays.
The implication: Harbrook's constraint was never model quality, it was alert-handling capacity — and the cheapest move may be to add review capacity, with or without the vendor.
A strong answer notes that the same logic should be applied to today's rules: are there alerts already being released unreviewed?
commonMistakes: Describing what changed in the exhibit rather than why it changes the decision.
Concluding that the vendor's system is good, when the finding is that capacity was the binding constraint.
Missing the follow-on question about whether to buy capacity instead of software.

questions.followUp: That is the argument the Chief Risk Officer needs on Thursday. Separately, the technology team has asked whether Harbrook should build its own screening model rather than license one.

questions.prompt: Choose the four pieces of data that, when combined, would allow us to estimate the net benefit of a model Harbrook builds itself, over the model's whole life. Assume the review team can handle every alert it raises.
options: Upfront cost to build, validate and get regulatory approval for the model
Number of years the model will stay effective before it must be rebuilt
Fraud value the model would prevent in each year of its life
Alert review cost in each year of the model's life
Cost of running, monitoring and retraining the model in each year of its life
The share of the model's alerts that turn out to be genuine fraud
The vendor's licence fee for the system Harbrook would otherwise buy

optionRationale: Needed. Lifetime net benefit is what the model delivers less what it cost to put in place.
Not needed. Three of the other items are already given 'in each year of its life', so the number of years is carried by them. Spending one of your four picks on it costs you a real input.
Needed, and per year: prevention will not be flat across the model's life as fraud patterns move.
Needed. Alerts are only worth raising if they are reviewed, and reviewing them costs money.
Needed. A model is not a one-off purchase; monitoring and retraining are the running cost of keeping it accurate.

Not needed here, though it is the first thing most people ask a vendor. The fraud prevented in each year already embeds how accurate the model is: picking this as well is asking for the same fact twice, and it costs you one of your four.
Not needed for this estimate. The vendor's fee is what you compare the answer against once you have it — it is not an input to the build's own benefit.
keyPoints: Lifetime net benefit = Σ over years of (fraud prevented − review cost − run and retrain cost) − upfront cost.
That expression consumes exactly the four selected items and nothing else.
A figure implied by another figure is not a missing input, and the alternative's price is not an input at all.
commonMistakes: Taking the number of years because a lifetime calculation obviously needs one, without noticing the per-year projections already carry it.
Taking the vendor licence fee because the case has been about the vendor throughout.
Estimating prevented fraud but forgetting that the model has to be run and retrained every year.

questions.followUp: Thanks. One last thing before the paper goes up.

questions.prompt: Your BCG project leader has asked you for the potential downsides of Harbrook relying on the new screening system — the things that could go wrong even if the arithmetic works. Could you share your thoughts in 3 to 4 lines?

keyPoints: False positives: a system that blocks three times as many transactions will decline more genuine ones, and declined customers stop using the card — a revenue and attrition cost that does not appear in the fraud numbers.
Model risk and explainability: a machine-learning model needs regulatory approval, monitoring and a documented rationale for each decline, and it drifts as fraud patterns change.
Dependence on the vendor: pricing power at renewal, and no in-house capability if the contract ends.
Operational risk in the offshore review arrangement — quality, turnover and data protection on the overflow alerts.
Fraudsters adapt: measured prevention rates decay once criminals learn what the new model catches.
commonMistakes: Listing generic technology-project risks with no connection to how fraud screening earns its money.
Missing the false-positive cost, which is the one risk that runs directly against the benefit just calculated.
Repeating the capacity argument instead of naming risks to the plan itself.

closing: That is everything. You separated what the system detects from what the bank can act on, found that the case turned on review capacity rather than model quality, and then watched the decision flip when that constraint was relieved. Thank you — the Chief Risk Officer gets the paper on Thursday.
